subject: biology
title: How enzymes work
key_idea: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts. A substrate fits the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex, and the enzyme lowers the activation energy of the reaction. The active site's tertiary structure makes each enzyme specific.

blocks.text: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of metabolism. This section covers what they are and where they work.

items.meaning: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
The region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place.
The molecule an enzyme acts on.
The temporary structure formed when a substrate is bound to the active site.
The minimum energy needed to start a reaction.

items: Enzymes are **globular proteins**. Their folded tertiary structure forms the active site.
**Intracellular enzymes** work inside cells. Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, a toxic product of metabolism, inside cells.
**Extracellular enzymes** are made in cells and secreted to work outside. Amylase digests starch in the gut.

Enzymes catalyse reactions at every level, from cell to whole organism. They affect **structure** (for example by building collagen and cell walls) and **function** (for example respiration and digestion).
Enzymes are globular proteins that catalyse metabolic reactions.
Intracellular enzymes work inside cells; extracellular enzymes are secreted.

sections.heading: Activation energy and the enzyme-substrate complex

blocks.text: A reaction needs a minimum energy to start. An enzyme provides a route with a lower activation energy.

diagram.alt: Energy against progress of reaction. The uncatalysed reaction has a high peak. The enzyme-catalysed reaction has a lower peak. Both start and end at the same energy levels.

items: The substrate binds to the active site, forming an **enzyme-substrate complex**.
Bonds in the substrate are strained or held in the correct position, so the reaction needs less energy.
The substrate is converted to product, forming an **enzyme-product complex**.
The product leaves, and the enzyme is unchanged and free to bind another substrate.

steps: Substrate collides with the active site

items: Enzymes lower the activation energy; they do not change the energy of reactants or products.
The enzyme is not used up and can be reused.

sections.heading: Specificity and models of enzyme action

blocks.text: Each enzyme normally catalyses one reaction. The shape and charges of its active site decide this.

items: The active site has a specific shape, set by the tertiary structure of the enzyme.
Only a substrate with a **complementary** shape and charges can bind. This is **specificity**.
A different primary structure gives a different tertiary structure and a different active site.

rows: The active site is a fixed shape, exactly complementary to the substrate.
The active site is flexible. It changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, so the R groups fit closely and strain the substrate's bonds.
Specificity, and also how binding lowers activation energy. Better fits the evidence.

items: The lock-and-key model came first. It was changed to the induced-fit model as new evidence showed that active sites are flexible.
Models of science change when new evidence does not fit the old model.
Specificity comes from the complementary shape of the active site.
Induced-fit is the current model: the active site moulds to the substrate.

checks.q: Explain how an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
checks.a: The substrate binds to the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex. This holds the substrate in position and strains its bonds, so less energy is needed to start the reaction.

checks.q: Explain why an enzyme is specific to one substrate.
checks.a: The enzyme's tertiary structure gives the active site a particular shape. Only a substrate with a complementary shape fits and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.

checks.q: Describe one difference between the lock-and-key and induced-fit models.
checks.a: In lock-and-key the active site is rigid and already complementary to the substrate. In induced-fit the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds, so it fits more closely.
